deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated notes. The second is a draft germ of Hilbert's 13th Problem; the next page continues it.

(A) VOTING ON SEVERAL MOTIONS (continued from the previous page)
- Setting. At the end of a debate there are n=3 motions A1, A2, A3. Each can be accepted or rejected, so the final outcome is one of 2^3 = 8 'possibilities' M1,...,M8 (M1 = all accepted, ..., M8 = all rejected).
- Axiom. Each voter's wishes form an ordered set: a strict total order on {M1,...,M8}. Hilbert states transitivity explicitly: if M2 is preferred to M3 and M3 to M4, then M2 is preferred to M4.
- Procedure. Each voter has ranked the 8 possibilities. Then at most 8 ballots (votes) determine 'which possibility is the wish of the assembly'. First vote M1 versus M2. If M1 wins, vote M1 versus M3, and so on: the winner of each round meets the next possibility.
- In modern terms this is a sequential pairwise-elimination agenda (a 'king of the hill' or successive procedure). Finding the maximum of 8 items this way takes exactly 8-1 = 7 comparisons.

(B) NOMOGRAPHY AND FUNCTIONS OF THREE VARIABLES
- d'Ocagne's claim (Traité de nomographie, 1899). Equations with more than 2 parameters, e.g. z = f of three variables, are in general not representable by drawn curves, even with arbitrarily many sheets of drawn curves.
- Hilbert's reading. The claim can only hold if one allows 'Curvenbüschel' (one-parameter families, pencils) and not 'Curvenbündel' (higher-parameter families, here 3-parameter). Otherwise it is trivially false.
- Counterexample sketch. Draw three parallel vertical lines carrying scales x, y, z. Through one point on each line (non-collinear) passes exactly one circle. Circles form a 3-parameter family: center (a,b) and radius r. So the map from circles to the triple (x,y,z) of their (lower) intersection heights is locally bijective. Labelling each circle with the value φ(x,y,z) therefore 'represents' an arbitrary function of three variables.
- The question. Do functions of x,y,z exist which cannot be generated by superposition of functions of two arguments? That is: substitute into a function of two arguments, then set each of these two arguments equal to functions of two arguments again, and so on, e.g. F(G(x,y), H(y,z)) and nested forms.
- Continuation (next page). Rational functions, ruler-and-compass functions, roots of equations of degree ≤5 and Abelian equations are all such superpositions. The root t of t^6 + x t^3 + y t^2 + z t + 1 = 0 is conjectured to be the simplest 'genuine' function of three variables. A footnote notes that every (continuous) function can be approximated by such superpositions, since rational functions can approximate it (Weierstrass), which suffices for nomography.
- This is the germ of Hilbert's 13th Problem (Paris, 1900). The published version uses the degree-7 resolvent x^7 + a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + 1 = 0 and explicitly cites d'Ocagne's nomography.

Implicit steps (mine):
- 8 = 2^3 because each of the 3 motions is independently accepted or rejected.
- Uniqueness of the circle: x^2 + Y^2 + D x + E Y + F = 0 through (a1,y1), (a2,y2), (a3,y3) is a linear system in D, E, F. Its determinant is that of the rows (a_i, y_i, 1), which is nonzero iff the three points are not collinear.
errors: Count: the sequential pairwise procedure on 8 alternatives needs exactly 7 votes, not 'at most 8'. This is harmless overcounting.

Substantive gap: transitivity of each individual's preferences does not imply that majority preference of the assembly is transitive (Condorcet paradox, 1785). With cyclic individual orders, the outcome of the successive pairwise procedure depends on the agenda order. 'The wish of the assembly' need not exist; it does if a Condorcet winner exists. Hilbert's argument tacitly assumes the collective preference is an ordering.

Circle construction: a vertical line generally meets a circle in two points, so one must fix a branch (e.g. the lower intersection) and restrict to circles meeting all three lines. Also, collinear triples correspond to no circle (a limiting line). These are minor and easily fixed; the point (Bündel vs Büschel) stands.

Interpretive: for continuous functions Hilbert's implicit expectation is wrong. Kolmogorov (1956) and Arnold (1957) showed every continuous function of 3 variables is a superposition of continuous functions of 2 (indeed of one variable plus addition). The question has substance only for algebraic or analytic/smooth classes. This error is on the next page / in the 1900 problem, not stated on this page.

results.what: Axiom that individual preferences over the 2^n outcomes of n binary motions form a (transitive) linear order, and determination of the assembly's choice by successive pairwise majority votes (winner stays on)
results.modern_name: Preference ordering axiom; successive pairwise-elimination (amendment / king-of-the-hill) agenda; outcome space of multi-issue voting
results.usually_credited_to: Condorcet (1785) and Borda for pairwise majority comparisons; the formal theory of agendas and social choice is due to Duncan Black (1948) and Kenneth Arrow (1951). The combinatorial multi-issue framing appears in later social-choice work.

results.what: Remark that with 3-parameter families of curves (e.g. circles cutting three parallel scales) any function of three variables can trivially be represented nomographically, so d'Ocagne's impossibility claim must be restricted to one-parameter families
results.modern_name: Nomographic representability / dimension counting of curve families
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert's 13th Problem (1900) discusses d'Ocagne's nomography; the related restriction remarks are part of nomography folklore

results.what: Question whether there exist functions of three variables not obtainable by superposition of functions of two arguments (draft of Hilbert's 13th problem)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (Paris ICM 1900); resolved for continuous functions by Kolmogorov (1956) and Arnold (1957)

deep.surprise_reason: The nomography passage is a known-type draft of Hilbert's 13th problem; its motivation from d'Ocagne is already explicit in the 1900 address. Seeing the pre-1900 drafting with the Büschel/Bündel distinction and the circle example (plus the sextic on the next page) is a nice archival detail, but not new mathematics. The voting note shows Hilbert axiomatizing collective decision procedures with an explicit transitivity axiom. That is a mildly interesting anticipation of social-choice formalism, but it misses the Condorcet problem, so it is mainly of historical curiosity.

checkable.asserts: Three accept/reject motions yield 8 possible outcomes M1..M8

checkable.sympy: a1,a2,a3,y1,y2,y3=symbols('a1 a2 a3 y1 y2 y3'); factor(Matrix([[a1,y1,1],[a2,y2,1],[a3,y3,1]]).det())
checkable.asserts: Determinant of the linear system for the circle x^2+Y^2+Dx+EY+F=0 through (a_i,y_i). It is nonzero iff the points are non-collinear, so a unique circle passes through one point on each of three lines (3-parameter family).

checkable.sympy: prefs=[[1,2,3],[2,3,1],[3,1,2]]; maj=lambda p,q: sum(1 for r in prefs if r.index(p)<r.index(q))>=2; [maj(1,2),maj(2,3),maj(3,1)]
checkable.asserts: Returns [True, True, True]: with transitive individual orders the majority relation can be cyclic (Condorcet paradox), so the assembly's 'wish' need not be an ordering.
Sequential pairwise elimination over 8 alternatives requires exactly 7 votes (Hilbert says at most 8).
